newsitem.title: USA: Report says Iraq still biological weapons threat.
newsitem.headline: Report says Iraq still biological weapons threat.

text.p: Iraq could reassamble its germ warfare programme within six months with a still-intact scientific team working with freeze-dried organisms, a former U.N. investigator said in a report published on Tuesday.
"The workforce of more than 200 persons who staffed Iraq's biological warfare programme is intact," Raymond Zilinskas said.
"Iraq's civilian biotechnological infrastructure, comprising more than 80 research, development and production facilities, is whole and well equipped," he added.
"It is prudent to assume that the Iraqis retain hidden stores of freeze-dried organisms from its former warfare programme," he said."

With those resources, he said, Iraq "could reconstitute a biological warfare programme rapidly and be able to manufacture militarily significant quantities of biological warfare agents within six months."

Zilinskas was a member of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) investigative team which along with the International Atomic Energy Agency has been overseeing the scrapping of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.

A researcher at the Centre for Public Issues in Biotechnology at the University of Maryland, his report was published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association -- an issue devoted to biological warfare problems.

Zilinskas said Iraq began its germ warfare programme in earnest in 1985 and developed anthrax, botulinum toxin -- the most toxic chemical known to science -- and one fungal strain that could be used against crops.

The actual threat from such weapons during the 1991 war was small because they were not produced in great quantity, the delivery systems were inefficient and the nature of the conflict limited Iraq's command and control capability, Zilinskas said.

"The Iraq of today is similar to Iraq before the Gulf War -- it has the same leader and form of governance, it possesses a large and powerful army and air force and it is able to deploy a large well-trained civilian workforce," he said.
"It is reasonable to assume that, as before, Iraq will attempt to overcome the numerical superiority of regional opponents by resorting to the use of weapons of mass destruction," Zilinskas said.
He suggestsed that UNSCOM "must remain fully operational until such time as a leadership is established in Iraq which poses no threat to its neighbours."
